explain.say: A drink can body is made from a single disc of aluminium with no seams. A press stamps thousands of discs a minute out of a wide coil of thin sheet.

explain.say: Next, the cup is rammed through a series of tight rings that stretch and thin the walls, called ironing. The walls end up about a tenth of a millimetre thick, like a sheet of paper, and the cup grows into a tall can.

explain.say: The base is pressed into a dome, which resists the pressure of a fizzy drink a bit like an arch. Then the can is trimmed, printed, narrowed at the top, filled, and a lid is sealed on by rolling the edges together.

faq.q: How is a can made without a seam?
faq.a: The body starts as one flat disc. A punch pushes it into a cup, then through ironing rings that stretch the walls upward, so bottom and sides are one piece. Only the lid is added separately.
asks: Why don't drink cans have a join down the side?

faq.q: Why are can walls so thin?
faq.a: Thin walls save aluminium, weight and money. They are strong enough because the drink's pressure pushes outwards evenly, stiffening the can like an inflated balloon. That is why an empty can crushes so easily.
asks: Why is an empty can easy to crush?

faq.q: Why do cans have a domed bottom?
faq.a: A flat bottom would bulge under the pressure of a fizzy drink. A dome pushed inwards spreads that force around, like an arch, so a thin base can hold several times the pressure of the air.
asks: Why is the bottom of a can curved?

faq.q: How is the lid put on a can?
faq.a: After filling, a lid is placed on top and rollers fold the edge of the lid and the can together into a tight double seam, sealed with a thin compound, all in a fraction of a second.

faq.q: Why are cans recycled so much?
faq.a: Aluminium can be melted and rolled into new sheet again and again, using only about 5 percent of the energy needed to make new metal. A recycled can can be back on the shelf in about two months.
asks: Can aluminium cans be recycled forever?

facts: A typical aluminium drink can weighs about 13 grams.
Coors introduced the first two-piece drawn-and-ironed aluminium drink can in 1959.
